name: reactive-architecture
context: Distributed systems requiring responsiveness, resilience, and elasticity under varying workloads. Reactive architecture builds systems where components communicate asynchronously via message-passing, enabling loose coupling, isolation, and location transparency.
benefits: Consistent response times under load through event-driven processing
Automatic scaling to handle traffic spikes
Low coupling between components through async messaging
Failure containment and recovery through supervision hierarchies
tradeoffs: Async programming harder to debug and reason about
avoid_when: Batch processing where latency is not critical
Predictable steady load without scaling needs
component_types: EventBus: Central channel for publishing and subscribing to events
MessageBroker: Intermediary that routes messages between producers and consumers
StreamProcessor: Processes data streams with back pressure support
CircuitBreaker: Prevents cascade failures by failing fast when a service is unhealthy
BackPressureManager: Controls producer rate to prevent consumer overwhelm
ServiceRegistry: Tracks location and health of service instances
Publisher: Emits data items to subscribers
Subscriber: Receives and processes data items
SupervisionHierarchy: Manages failure recovery through parent-child actor relationships
anti_patterns: Distributed monolith (reactive facade over blocking core)
Ignoring back pressure (leads to memory overflow)
design_principles: Message-Driven Communication: Components communicate via asynchronous messages, creating temporal and spatial decoupling
Location Transparency: Components can be replicated and moved without changing code, enabling elastic scaling
Failure Isolation: Each component fails independently; failures are contained and managed through supervision hierarchies
Non-Blocking I/O: Resource utilization optimized through asynchronous, non-blocking operations
Back Pressure: Consumers control the rate of production to prevent overwhelm
Elasticity: System automatically scales up and down based on workload
Responsiveness: System responds in a timely manner under all conditions
Supervision Hierarchies: Parent components manage child component failures through defined strategies
best_practices: Incremental Adoption: Start with non-critical features; don't rewrite entire system at once
Anti-Corruption Layer: Bridge legacy blocking code with reactive world using adapters
Back Pressure Handling: Always implement back pressure to prevent memory overflow
Circuit Breaker Configuration: Set appropriate failure thresholds and timeout values
Failure Handling: Design for failure from the start; implement retries, fallbacks, and compensation
Observability: Add comprehensive metrics, tracing, and logging at each component
Schema Evolution: Design event schemas for backward and forward compatibility
Resource Management: Use connection pooling and bounded queues to prevent resource exhaustion
Testing: Use StepVerifier and embedded brokers for comprehensive reactive testing
Avoid Blocking: Never call blocking operations (like JDBC) in reactive threads; use R2DBC instead
